entries.5ac433a87ff1f285d8f8b58fff2668ddd8908507: <div sID="gen397" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Gen.10" sID="Gen.10"/> <div eID="gen397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen398" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen399" type="x-p"/> This chapter shows more particularly what was said in general (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.19">ch. ix. 19</reference>), concerning the three sons of Noah, that "of them was the whole earth overspread;" and the fruit of that blessing (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.1">ch. ix. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.9.7">7</reference>), "replenish the earth." Is is the only certain account extant of the origin of nations; and yet perhaps there is no nation but that of the Jews that can be confident from which of these seventy fountains (for so many there are here) it derives its streams. Through the want of early records, the mixtures of people, the revolutions of nations, and distance of time, the knowledge of the lineal descent of the present inhabitants of the earth is lost; nor were any genealogies preserved but those of the Jews, for the sake of the Messiah, only in this chapter we have a brief account, I. Of the posterity of Japheth, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.2-Gen.10.5">ver. 2-5</reference>. II. The posterity of Ham (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.6-Gen.10.20">ver. 6-20</reference>), and in this particular notice is taken of Nimrod, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.8-Gen.10.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. III. The posterity of Shem, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.21-Gen.10.32">ver. 21</reference>, &c.
entries.b2027262987eb3c3d47aee0fb35493f78a7bf214: <div eID="gen399" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen398" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Generations of Noah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 2347.)</title> <div sID="gen400" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the generations of the sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth: and unto them were sons born after the flood. <hi type="super">2</hi> The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the sons of Gomer; Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the sons of Javan; Elishah, and Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. <hi type="super">5</hi> By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands; every one after his tongue, after their families, in their nations. <div eID="gen400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen401" type="x-p"/> Moses begins with Japheth's family, either because he was the eldest, or because his family lay remotest from Israel and had least concern with them at the time when Moses wrote, and therefore he mentions that race very briefly, hastening to give an account of the posterity of Ham, who were Israel's enemies and of Shem, who were Israel's ancestors; for it is the church that the scripture is designed to be the history of, and of the nations of the world only as they were some way or other related to Israel and interested in the affairs of Israel. Observe, 1. Notice is taken that the sons of Noah had sons born to them after the flood, to repair and rebuild the world of mankind which the flood had ruined. He that had killed now makes alive. 2. The posterity of Japheth were allotted to the isles of the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.5">v. 5</reference>), which were solemnly, by lot, after a survey, divided among them, and probably this island of ours among the rest; all places beyond the sea from Judea are called <hi type="italic">isles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.22">Jer. xxv. 22</reference>), and this directs us to understand that promise (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.4">Isa. xlii. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">the isles shall wait for his law,</hi> of the conversion of the Gentiles to the faith of Christ.
entries.dae9e130c16be770c5ef9bce1374abf0e44641d3: <div eID="gen401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen402" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And the sons of Ham; Cush, and Mizraim, and Phut, and Canaan. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the sons of Cush; Seba, and Havilah, and Sabtah, and Raamah, and Sabtecha: and the sons of Raamah; Sheba, and Dedan. <hi type="super">8</hi> And Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth. <hi type="super">9</hi> He was a mighty hunter before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : wherefore it is said; Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">10</hi> And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. <hi type="super">11</hi> Out of that land went forth Asshur, and builded Nineveh, and the city Rehoboth, and Calah, <hi type="super">12</hi> And Resen between Nineveh and Calah: the same <hi type="italic">is</hi> a great city. 13 And Mizraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim, <hi type="super">14</hi> And Pathrusim, and Casluhim, (out of whom came Philistim,) and Caphtorim. <div eID="gen402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen403" type="x-p"/> That which is observable and improvable in these verses is the account here given of Nimrod, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.8-Gen.10.10">v. 8-10</reference>. He is here represented as a great man in his day: <hi type="italic">He began to be a mighty one in the earth,</hi> that is, whereas those that went before him were content to stand upon the same level with their neighbours, and though every man bore rule in his own house yet no man pretended any further, Nimrod's aspiring mind could not rest here; he was resolved to tower above his neighbours, not only to be eminent among them, but to lord it over them. The same spirit that actuated the giants before the flood (who became <hi type="italic">mighty men, and men of renown,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.6.4">ch. vi. 4</reference>), now revived in him, so soon was that tremendous judgment which the pride and tyranny of those mighty men brought upon the world forgotten. Note, There are some in whom ambition and affectation of dominion seem to be bred in the bone; such there have been and will be, notwithstanding the wrath of God often revealed from heaven against them. Nothing on this side hell will humble and break the proud spirits of some men, in this like Lucifer, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.14-Isa.14.15">Isa. xiv. 14, 15</reference>. Now, <div eID="gen403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen404" type="x-p"/> I. Nimrod was a great hunter; with this he began, and for this became famous to a proverb. Every great hunter is, in remembrance of him, called a <hi type="italic">Nimrod.</hi> 1. Some think he did good with his hunting, served his country by ridding it of the wild beasts which infested it, and so insinuated himself into the affections of his neighbours, and got to be their prince. Those that exercise authority either are, or at least would be called, <hi type="italic">benefactors,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.22.25">Luke xxii. 25</reference>. 2. Others think that under pretence of hunting he gathered men under his command, in pursuit of another game he had to play, which was to make himself master of the country and to bring them into subjection. He was a <hi type="italic">mighty hunter,</hi> that is, he was a violent invader of his neighbours' rights and properties, and a persecutor of innocent men, carrying all before him, and endeavouring to make all his own by force and violence. He thought himself a mighty prince, but <hi type="italic">before the Lord</hi> (that is, in God's account) he was but a <hi type="italic">mighty hunter.</hi> Note, Great conquerors are but great hunters. Alexander and Cesar would not make such a figure in scripture-history as they do in common history; the former is represented in prophecy but as a he-goat pushing, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.5">Dan. viii. 5</reference>. Nimrod was a mighty hunter <hi type="italic">against</hi> the Lord, so the LXX; that is, (1.) He set up idolatry, as Jeroboam did, for the confirming of his usurped dominion. That he might set up a new government, he set up a new religion upon the ruin of the primitive constitution of both. <hi type="italic">Babel was the mother of harlots.</hi> Or, (2.) He carried on his oppression and violence in defiance of God himself, daring Heaven with his impieties, as if he and his huntsmen could out-brave the Almighty, and were a match for the Lord of hosts and all his armies. <hi type="italic">As if it were a small thing to weary men, he thinks to weary my God also,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.7.13">Isa. vii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen405" type="x-p"/> II. Nimrod was a great ruler: <hi type="italic">The beginning of his kingdom was Babel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.10.10">v. 10</reference>. Some way or other, by arts or arms, he got into power, either being chosen to it or forcing his way to it; and so laid the foundations of a monarchy, which was afterwards a head of gold, and the terror of the mighty, and bade fair to be universal. It does not appear that he had any right to rule by birth; but either his fitness for government recommended him, as some think, to an election, or by power and policy he advanced gradually, and perhaps insensibly, into the throne. See the antiquity of civil government, and particularly that form of it which lodges the sovereignty in a single person. If Nimrod and his neighbours began, other nations soon learned to incorporate under one head for their common safety and welfare, which, however it began, proved so great a blessing to the world that things were reckoned to go ill indeed when there <hi type="italic">was no king in Israel.</hi> <div eID="gen405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen406" type="x-p"/> III. Nimrod was a great builder. Probably he was architect in the building of Babel, and there he began his kingdom; but, when his project to rule all the sons of Noah was baffled by the confusion of tongues, <hi type="italic">out of that land he went forth into Assyria</hi> (so the margin reads it, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.11">v. 11</reference>) <hi type="italic">and built Nineveh,</hi> &c., that, having built these cities, he might command them and rule over them. Observe, in Nimrod, the nature of ambition. 1. It is boundless. Much would have more, and still cries, <hi type="italic">Give, give.</hi> 2. It is restless. Nimrod, when he had four cities under his command, could not be content till he had four more. 3. It is expensive. Nimrod will rather be at the charge of rearing cities than not have the honour of ruling them. The spirit of building is the common effect of a spirit of pride. 4. It is daring, and will stick at nothing. Nimrod's name signifies rebellion, which (if indeed he did abuse his power to the oppression of his neighbours) teaches us that tyrants to men are rebels to God, and their <hi type="italic">rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft.</hi>
entries.26570454030db189fa65d36dea97032a96f886e3: <div eID="gen406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen407" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And Canaan begat Sidon his firstborn, and Heth, <hi type="super">16</hi> And the Jebusite, and the Amorite, and the Girgasite, <hi type="super">17</hi> And the Hivite, and the Arkite, and the Sinite, <hi type="super">18</hi> And the Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite: and afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the border of the Canaanites was from Sidon, as thou comest to Gerar, unto Gaza; as thou goest, unto Sodom, and Gomorrah, and Admah, and Zeboim, even unto Lasha. <hi type="super">20</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Ham, after their families, after their tongues, in their countries, <hi type="italic">and</hi> in their nations. <div eID="gen407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen408" type="x-p"/> Observe here, 1. The account of the posterity of Canaan, of the families and nations that descended from him, and of the land they possessed, is more particular than of any other in this chapter, because these were the nations that were to be subdued before Israel, and their land was in process of time to become the holy land, <hi type="italic">Immanuel's land;</hi> and this God had an eye to when, in the meantime, he cast the lot of that accursed devoted race in that spot of ground which he had selected for his own people; this Moses takes notice of, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.8">Deut. xxxii. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">When the Most High divided to the nations their inheritance, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel.</hi> 2. By this account it appears that the posterity of Canaan were numerous, and rich, and very pleasantly situated; and yet Canaan was under a curse, a divine curse, and not a curse causeless. Note, Those that are under the curse of God may yet perhaps thrive and prosper greatly in this world; for we cannot know love or hatred, the blessing or the curse, by what is before us, but by what is within us, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.1">Eccl. ix. 1</reference>. The curse of God always works really and always terribly: but perhaps it is a secret curse, a curse to the soul, and does not work visibly, or a slow curse, and does not work immediately; but sinners are by it reserved for, and bound over to, a day of wrath. Canaan here has a better land than either Shem or Japheth, and yet they have a better lot, for they inherit the blessing.
entries.a00459287895d14712e2a7b9236a7e5b89056b0a: <div eID="gen408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen409" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Unto Shem also, the father of all the children of Eber, the brother of Japheth the elder, even to him were <hi type="italic">children</hi> born. <hi type="super">22</hi> The children of Shem; Elam, and Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram. <hi type="super">23</hi> And the children of Aram; Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash. <hi type="super">24</hi> And Arphaxad begat Salah; and Salah begat Eber. <hi type="super">25</hi> And unto Eber were born two sons: the name of one <hi type="italic">was</hi> Peleg; for in his days was the earth divided; and his brother's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Joktan. <hi type="super">26</hi> And Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah, <hi type="super">27</hi> And Hadoram, and Uzal, and Diklah, <hi type="super">28</hi> And Obal, and Abimael, and Sheba, <hi type="super">29</hi> And Ophir, and Havilah, and Jobab: all these <hi type="italic">were</hi> the sons of Joktan. <hi type="super">30</hi> And their dwelling was from Mesha, as thou goest unto Sephar a mount of the east. <hi type="super">31</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Shem, after their families, after their tongues, in their lands, after their nations. <hi type="super">32</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations: and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood. <div eID="gen409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen410" type="x-p"/> Two things especially are observable in this account of the posterity of Shem:— <div eID="gen410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen411" type="x-p"/> I. The description of Shem, v. 21. We have not only his name, <hi type="italic">Shem,</hi> which signifies <hi type="italic">a name,</hi> but two titles to distinguish him by:— <div eID="gen411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen412" type="x-p"/> 1. He was <hi type="italic">the father of all the children of Eber.</hi> Eber was his great grandson; but why should he be called the father of all <hi type="italic">his</hi> children, rather than of all Arphaxad's, or Salah's, &c.? Probably because Abraham and his seed, God's covenant-people, not only descended from Heber, but from him were called <hi type="italic">Hebrews;</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.14.13">ch. xiv. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">Abram the Hebrew.</hi> Paul looked upon it as his privilege that he was a <hi type="italic">Hebrew of the Hebrews,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.5">Phil. iii. 5</reference>. Eber himself, we may suppose, was a man eminent for religion in a time of general apostasy, and a great example of piety to his family; and, the holy tongue being commonly called from him the <hi type="italic">Hebrew,</hi> it is probable that he retained it in his family, in the confusion of Babel, as a special token of God's favour to him; and from him the professors of religion were called <hi type="italic">the children of Eber.</hi> Now, when the inspired penman would give Shem an honourable title, he calls him <hi type="italic">the father of the Hebrews.</hi> Though when Moses wrote this, they were a poor despised people, bond-slaves in Egypt, yet, being God's people, it was an honour to a man to be akin to them. As Ham, though he had many sons, is disowned by being called <hi type="italic">the father of Canaan,</hi> on whose seed the <hi type="italic">curse</hi> was entailed (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.22">ch. ix. 22</reference>), so Shem, though he had many sons, is dignified with the title of <hi type="italic">the father of Eber,</hi> on whose seed the blessing was entailed. Note, a family of saints is more truly honourable than a family of nobles, Shem's holy seed than Ham's royal seed, Jacob's twelve patriarchs than Ishmael's twelve princes, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.20">ch. xvii. 20</reference>. Goodness is true greatness. <div eID="gen412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen413" type="x-p"/> 2. He was <hi type="italic">the brother of Japheth the elder,</hi> by which it appears that, though Shem is commonly put first, he was not Noah's first-born, but Japheth was older. But why should this also be put as part of Shem's title and description, that he <hi type="italic">was the brother of Japheth,</hi> since it had been, in effect, said often before? And was he not as much brother to Ham? Probably this was intended to signify the union of the Gentiles with the Jews in the church. The sacred historian had mentioned it as Shem's honour that he was the father of the Hebrews; but, lest Japheth's seed should therefore be looked upon as for ever shut out from the church, he here reminds us that he <hi type="italic">was the brother of Japheth,</hi> not in birth only, but in blessing; for <hi type="italic">Japheth was to dwell in the tents of Shem.</hi> Note, (1.) Those are brethren in the best manner that are so by grace, and that meet in the covenant of God and in the communion of saints. (2.) God, in dispensing his grace, does not go by seniority, but the younger sometimes gets the start of the elder in coming into the church; <hi type="italic">so the last shall be first and the first last.</hi> <div eID="gen413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen414" type="x-p"/> II. The reason of the name of Peleg (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.25">v. 25</reference>): Because <hi type="italic">in his days</hi> (that is, about the time of his birth, when his name was given him), <hi type="italic">was the earth divided</hi> among the children of men that were to inhabit it; either when Noah divided it by an orderly distribution of it, as Joshua divided the land of Canaan by lot, or when, upon their refusal to comply with that division, God, in justice, divided them by the confusion of tongues: whichsoever of these was the occasion, pious Heber saw cause to perpetuate the remembrance of it in the name of his son; and justly may our sons be called by the same name, for in our days, in another sense, is the earth, the church, most wretchedly divided.  <chapter eID="Gen.10"/> <div eID="gen414" type="x-p"/>

entries.1a9a5358f51f5c7bdd2d41b36de5933e14cc89c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv122"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.10.1-Gen.10.32">Ge 10:1-32</reference>. Genealogies.</title> <div sID="gen270" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv122"/><hi type="bold">1. sons of Noah--</hi>The historian has not arranged this catalogue according to seniority of birth; for the account begins with the descendants of Japheth, and the line of Ham is given before that of Shem though he is expressly said to be the youngest or younger son of Noah; and Shem was the elder brother of Japheth (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.21">Ge 10:21</reference>), the true rendering of that passage.<div eID="gen270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen271" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">generations, &c.--</hi>the narrative of the settlement of nations existing in the time of Moses, perhaps only the principal ones; for though the list comprises the sons of Shem, Ham, and Japheth, all their descendants are not enumerated. Those descendants, with one or two exceptions, are described by names indicative of tribes and nations and ending in the Hebrew im, or the English "-ite." <div eID="gen271" type="x-p"/>
entries.7732a1055df929b2bc8ffcd6b5f5f1b997c494fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv123"/><div sID="gen272" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv123"/><hi type="bold">5. the isles of the Gentiles--</hi>a phrase by which the Hebrews described all countries which were accessible by sea (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.11">Is 11:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.20.6">20:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.22">Jr 25:22</reference>). Such in relation to them were the countries of Europe, the peninsula of Lesser Asia, and the region lying on the east of the Euxine. Accordingly, it was in these quarters the early descendants of Japheth had their settlements. <div eID="gen272" type="x-p"/>
entries.430d4d1107b960709ca5c9825e6e6dd676b28a47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv124"/><div sID="gen273" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv124"/><hi type="bold">6. sons of Ham--</hi>emigrated southward, and their settlements were: Cush in Arabia, Canaan in the country known by his name, and Mizraim in Egypt, Upper and Lower. It is generally thought that his father accompanied him and personally superintended the formation of the settlement, whence Egypt was called "the land of Ham" [Psa 105:23, 27; 106:22]. <div eID="gen273" type="x-p"/>
entries.90184a4cf671501344828428be9752466afb19ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv125"/><div sID="gen274" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv125"/><hi type="bold">8. Nimrod--</hi>mentioned as eclipsing all his family in renown. He early distinguished himself by his daring and successful prowess in hunting wild beasts. By those useful services he earned a title to public gratitude; and, having established a permanent ascendancy over the people, he founded the first kingdom in the world [Ge 10:10]. <div eID="gen274" type="x-p"/>
entries.0bd12f9585569d38b6c904cbc4938e4f388acf33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv126"/><div sID="gen275" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv126"/><hi type="bold">10. the beginning of his kingdom--</hi>This kingdom, of course, though then considered great, would be comparatively limited in extent, and the towns but small forts. <div eID="gen275" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ce3ec7c0a5277775f8b0f02ab7130091fe420ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv127"/><div sID="gen276" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv127"/><hi type="bold">11. Out of that land went forth Asshur--</hi>or, as the Margin has it, "He [Nimrod] at the head of his army went forth into Assyria," that is, he pushed his conquests into that country.<div eID="gen276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and builded Nineveh--</hi>opposite the town of Mosul, on the Tigris, and the other towns near it. This raid into Assyria was an invasion of the territories of Shem, and hence the name "Nimrod," signifying "rebel," is supposed to have been conferred on him from his daring revolt against the divine distribution. <div eID="gen277" type="x-p"/>
entries.f751b13bc0b10e6be51c78319f6c4c8c47bb6d25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv128"/><div sID="gen278" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv128"/><hi type="bold">21. Unto Shem--</hi>The historian introduces him with marked distinction as "the father of Eber," the ancestor of the Hebrews. <div eID="gen278" type="x-p"/>
entries.6592af0a20fb52aa2f4056f351672371c3fc7e67: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv129"/><div sID="gen279" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv129"/><hi type="bold">23. Aram--</hi>In the general division of the earth, the countries of Armenia, Mesopotamia, and Syria, fell to his descendants. <div eID="gen279" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1cfd26962c516bbf252ef5ab3d55ddda46c3f5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv130"/><div sID="gen280" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv130"/><hi type="bold">24. Arphaxad--</hi>The settlement of his posterity was in the extensive valley of Shinar, on the Tigris, towards the southern extremity of Mesopotamia, including the country of Eden and the region on the east side of the river. <div eID="gen280" type="x-p"/>
entries.690e568b1336bc74112b3609bc700de6d66a9aa2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv131"/><div sID="gen281" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv131"/><hi type="bold">25. Peleg; for in his days was the earth divided--</hi>After the flood (<reference osisRef="Gen.11.10-Gen.11.16">Ge 11:10-16</reference>) the descendants of Noah settled at pleasure and enjoyed the produce of the undivided soil. But according to divine instruction, made probably through Eber, who seems to have been distinguished for piety or a prophetic character, the earth was divided and his son's name, "Peleg," was given in memory of that event (see <reference osisRef="Deut.32.8">De 32:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.26">Ac 17:26</reference>). <div eID="gen281" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4e499afbf029e022d5a495dc15581effdfe73db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv132"/><div sID="gen282" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv132"/><hi type="bold">32. These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations, &c.--</hi>This division was made in the most orderly manner; and the inspired historian evidently intimates that the sons of Noah were ranged according to their nations, and every nation ranked by its families, so that every nation had its assigned territory, and in every nation the tribes, and in every tribe the families, were located by themselves. <chapter eID="Gen.10"/>

entries.581d1ef0b1a59b9a446ff7e1f97efd4a453dfedf: <div eID="gen468" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen469" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen470" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen470" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen469" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen471" type="x-p"/> The generations of the sons of Noah, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.1">Gen 10:1</reference>. Japheth and his descendants, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.2-Gen.10.4">Gen 10:2-4</reference>. The isles of the Gentiles, or Europe, peopled by the Japhethites, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.5">Gen 10:5</reference>. Ham and his posterity, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.6-Gen.10.20">Gen 10:6-20</reference>. Nimrod, one of his descendants, a mighty hunter, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.8">Gen 10:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.9">Gen 10:9</reference>, founds the first kingdom, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.10">Gen 10:10</reference>. Nineveh and other cities founded, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.11">Gen 10:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.12">Gen 10:12</reference>. The Canaanites in their nine grand branches or families, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.15-Gen.10.18">Gen 10:15-18</reference>. Their territories, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.19">Gen 10:19</reference>. Shem and his posterity, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.21-Gen.10.31">Gen 10:21-31</reference>. The earth divided in the days of Peleg, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.25">Gen 10:25</reference>. The territories of the Shemites, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.30">Gen 10:30</reference>. The whole earth peopled by the descendants of Noah's three sons, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.32">Gen 10:32</reference>. <div eID="gen471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen472" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen473" type="x-p"/> Now these are the generations - It is extremely difficult to say what particular nations and people sprang from the three grand divisions of the family of Noah, because the names of many of those ancient people have become changed in the vast lapse of time from the deluge to the Christian era; yet some are so very distinctly marked that they can be easily ascertained, while a few still retain their original names. <div eID="gen473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen474" type="x-p"/> Moses does not always give the name of the first settler in a country, but rather that of the people from whom the country afterwards derived its name. Thus Mizraim is the dual of Mezer, and could never be the name of an individual. The like may be said of Kittim, Dodanim, Ludim, Ananim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim, Philistim, and Caphtorim, which are all plurals, and evidently not the names of individuals, but of families or tribes. See <reference osisRef="Gen.10.4">Gen 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Gen 10:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.13">Gen 10:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.14">Gen 10:14</reference>. <div eID="gen474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen475" type="x-p"/> In the posterity of Canaan we find whole nations reckoned in the genealogy, instead of the individuals from whom they sprang; thus the Jebusite, Amorite, Girgasite, Hivite, Arkite, Sinite, Arvadite, Zemarite, and Hamathite, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.16-Gen.10.18">Gen 10:16-18</reference>, were evidently whole nations or tribes which inhabited the promised land, and were called Canaanites from Canaan, the son of Ham, who settled there. Moses also, in this genealogy, seems to have introduced even the name of some places that were remarkable in the sacred history, instead of the original settlers. Such as Hazarmaveth, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.26">Gen 10:26</reference>; and probably Ophir and Havilah, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.29">Gen 10:29</reference>. But this is not infrequent in the sacred writings, as may be seen <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.51">1Chr 2:51</reference>, where Salma is called the father of Bethlehem, which certainly never was the name of a man, but of a place sufficiently celebrated in the sacred history; and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.14">1Chr 4:14</reference>, where Joab is called the father of the valley of Charashim, which no person could ever suppose was intended to designate an individual, but the society of craftsmen or artificers who lived there. <div eID="gen475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen476" type="x-p"/> Eusebius and others state (from what authority we know not) that Noah was commanded of God to make a will and bequeath the whole of the earth to his three sons and their descendants in the following manner: - To Shem, all the East; to Ham, all Africa; to Japheth, the Continent of Europe with its isles, and the northern parts of Asia. See the notes at the end of the preceding chapter, <reference osisRef="Gen.9.29">Gen 9:29</reference> (note).
entries.9eb8e557dfe8cad44cf77efc84af2f3cc45214b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen477" type="x-p"/> The sons of Japheth - Japheth is supposed to be the same with the Japetus of the Greeks, from whom, in an extremely remote antiquity, that people were supposed to have derived their origin. <div eID="gen477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen478" type="x-p"/> Gomer - Supposed by some to have peopled Galatia; so Josephus, who says that the Galatians were anciently named Gomerites. From him the Cimmerians or Cimbrians are supposed to have derived their origin. <div eID="gen478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen479" type="x-p"/> Bochart has no doubt that the Phrygians sprang from this person, and some of our principal commentators are of the same opinion. <div eID="gen479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen480" type="x-p"/> Magog - Supposed by many to be the father of the Scythians and Tartars, or Tatars, as the word should be written; and in great Tartary many names are still found which bear such a striking resemblance to the Gog and Magog of the Scriptures, as to leave little doubt of their identity. <div eID="gen480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen481" type="x-p"/> Madai - Generally supposed to be the progenitor of the Medes; but Joseph Mede makes it probable that he was rather the founder of a people in Macedonia called Maedi, and that Macedonia was formerly called Emathia, a name formed from Ei, an island, and Madai, because he and his descendants inhabited the maritime coast on the borders of the Ionian Sea. On this subject nothing certain can be advanced. <div eID="gen481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen482" type="x-p"/> Javan - It is almost universally agreed that from him sprang the Ionians, of Asia Minor; but this name seems to have been anciently given to the Macedonians, Achaians, and Baeotians. <div eID="gen482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen483" type="x-p"/> Tubal - Some think be was the father of the Iberians, and that a part at least of Spain was peopled by him and his descendants; and that Meshech, who is generally in Scripture joined with him, was the founder of the Cappadocians, from whom proceeded the Muscovites. <div eID="gen483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen484" type="x-p"/> Tiras - From this person, according to general consent, the Thracians derived their origin.
entries.40298f851af69c13daa01219099cc5609d09895d: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen485" type="x-p"/> Ashkenaz - Probably gave his name to Sacagena, a very excellent province of Armenia. Pliny mentions a people called Ascanitici, who dwelt about the Tanais and the Palus Maeotis; and some suppose that from Ashkenaz the Euxine Sea derived its name, but others suppose that from him the Germans derived their origin. <div eID="gen485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen486" type="x-p"/> Riphath - Or Diphath, the founder of the Paphlagonians, which were anciently called Riphataei. <div eID="gen486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen487" type="x-p"/> Togarmah - The Sauromates, or inhabitants of Turcomania. See the reasons in Calmet.
entries.e78517b1b8a32a88031583ffb792d695e28b5f2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen488" type="x-p"/> Elishah - As Javan peopled a considerable part of Greece, it is in that region that we must seek for the settlements of his descendants; Elishah probably was the first who settled at Elis, in Peloponnesus. <div eID="gen488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen489" type="x-p"/> Tarshish - He first inhabited Cilicia, whose capital anciently was the city of Tarsus, where the Apostle Paul was born. <div eID="gen489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen490" type="x-p"/> Kittim - We have already seen that this name was rather the name of a people than of an individual: some think by Kittim Cyprus is meant: others, the isle of Chios; and others, the Romans; and others, the Macedonians. <div eID="gen490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen491" type="x-p"/> Dodanim - Or Rodanim, for the ד and ר may be easily mistaken for each other, because of their great similarity. Some suppose that this family settled at Dodona in Epirus; others at the isle of Rhodes; others, at the Rhone, in France, the ancient name of which was Rhodanus, from the Scripture Rodanim.
entries.3c98c10f4fac9d0ae08c648250deb8f07403bce0: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen492" type="x-p"/> Isles of the Gentiles - Europe, of which this is allowed to be a general epithet. Calmet supposes that it comprehends all those countries to which the Hebrews were obliged to go by sea, such as Spain, Gaul, Italy, Greece, and Asia Minor. <div eID="gen492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen493" type="x-p"/> Every one after his tongue - This refers to the time posterior to the confusion of tongues and dispersion from Babel.
entries.8a70f2ee1427f7b82cd2b894ecd6a6dca665cedf: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen494" type="x-p"/> Cush - Who peopled the Arabic nome near the Red Sea in Lower Egypt. Some think the Ethiopians descended from him. <div eID="gen494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen495" type="x-p"/> Mizraim - This family certainly peopled Egypt; and both in the East and in the West, Egypt is called Mezr and Mezraim. <div eID="gen495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen496" type="x-p"/> Phut - Who first peopled an Egyptian nome or district, bordering on Libya. <div eID="gen496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen497" type="x-p"/> Canaan - He who first peopled the land so called, known also by the name of the Promised Land.
entries.1752d29a5c442c4066039cf2c1d26f2d13fbfced: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen498" type="x-p"/> Seba - The founder of the Sabaeans. There seem to be three different people of this name mentioned in this chapter, and a fourth in <reference osisRef="Gen.25.3">Gen 25:3</reference>. <div eID="gen498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen499" type="x-p"/> Havilah - Supposed by some to mean the inhabitants of the country included within that branch of the river Pison which ran out of the Euphrates into the bay of Persia, and bounded Arabia Felix on the east. <div eID="gen499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen500" type="x-p"/> Sabtah - Supposed by some to have first peopled an isle or peninsula called Saphta, in the Persian Gulf. <div eID="gen500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen501" type="x-p"/> Raamah - Or Ragmah, for the word is pronounced both ways, because of the ע ain, which some make a vowel, and some a consonant. Ptolemy mentions a city called Regma near the Persian Gulf; it probably received its name from the person in the text. <div eID="gen501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen502" type="x-p"/> Sabtechah - From the river called Samidochus, in Caramanla; Bochart conjectures that the person in the text fixed his residence in that part. <div eID="gen502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen503" type="x-p"/> Sheba - Supposed to have had his residence beyond the Euphrates, in the environs of Charran, Eden, etc. <div eID="gen503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen504" type="x-p"/> Dedan - Supposed to have peopled a part of Arabia, on the confines of Idumea.
entries.024d6c1867517c0a4c3161b87c259354b77ee346: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen505" type="x-p"/> Nimrod - Of this person little is known, as he is not mentioned except here and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.10">1Chr 1:10</reference>, which is evidently a copy of the text in Genesis. He is called a mighty hunter before the Lord; and from <reference osisRef="Gen.10.10">Gen 10:10</reference>, we learn that he founded a kingdom which included the cities Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. Though the words are not definite, it is very likely he was a very bad man. His name Nimrod comes from מרד, marad, he rebelled; and the Targum, on <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.10">1Chr 1:10</reference>, says: Nimrod began to be a mighty man in sin, a murderer of innocent men, and a rebel before the Lord. The Jerusalem Targum says: "He was mighty in hunting (or in prey) and in sin before God, for he was a hunter of the children of men in their languages; and he said unto them, Depart from the religion of Shem, and cleave to the institutes of Nimrod." The Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel says: "From the foundation of the world none was ever found like Nimrod, powerful in hunting, and in rebellions against the Lord." The Syriac calls him a warlike giant. The word ציד tsayid, which we render hunter, signifies prey; and is applied in the Scriptures to the hunting of men by persecution, oppression, and tyranny. Hence it is likely that Nimrod, having acquired power, used it in tyranny and oppression; and by rapine and violence founded that domination which was the first distinguished by the name of a kingdom on the face of the earth. How many kingdoms have been founded in the same way, in various ages and nations from that time to the present! From the Nimrods of the earth, God deliver the world! <div eID="gen505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen506" type="x-p"/> Mr. Bryant, in his Mythology, considers Nimrod as the principal instrument of the idolatry that afterwards prevailed in the family of Cush, and treats him as an arch rebel and apostate. Mr. Richardson, who was the determined foe of Mr. Bryant's whole system, asks, Dissertation, p. 405, "Where is the authority for these aspersions? They are nowhere to be discovered in the originals, in the versions, nor in the paraphrases of the sacred writings." If they are not to be found either in versions or paraphrases of the sacred writings, the above quotations are all false.
entries.b2a120114d41a0edef4f698405be0eeb2c19f78a: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen507" type="x-p"/> The beginning of his kingdom was Babel - בבל babel signifies confusion; and it seems to have been a very proper name for the commencement of a kingdom that appears to have been founded in apostasy from God, and to have been supported by tyranny, rapine, and oppression. <div eID="gen507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen508" type="x-p"/> In the land of Shinar - The same as mentioned <reference osisRef="Gen.11.2">Gen 11:2</reference>. It appears that, as Babylon was built on the river Euphrates, and the tower of Babel was in the land of Shinar, consequently Shinar itself must have been in the southern part of Mesopotamia.
entries.647d04decb1593a2c8c1cf358b3e269901a80d15: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen509" type="x-p"/> Out of that land went forth Asshur - The marginal reading is to be preferred here. He - Nimrod, went out into Assyria and built Nineveh; and hence Assyria is called the land of Nimrod, <reference osisRef="Mic.5.6">Mic 5:6</reference>. Thus did this mighty hunter extend his dominions in every possible way. The city of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, is supposed to have had its name from Ninus, the son of Nimrod; but probably Ninus and Nimrod are the same person. This city, which made so conspicuous a figure in the history of the world, is now called Mossul; it is an inconsiderable place, built out of the ruins of the ancient Nineveh. <div eID="gen509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen510" type="x-p"/> Rehoboth, and Calah, etc. - Nothing certain is known concerning the situation of these places; conjecture is endless, and it has been amply indulged by learned men in seeking for Rehoboth in the Birtha of Ptolemy, Calah in Calachine, Resen in Larissa, etc., etc.
entries.b1978842848f7ab34735601bb815e691f37c4134: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen511" type="x-p"/> Mizraim begat Ludim - Supposed to mean the inhabitants of the Mareotis, a canton in Egypt, for the name Ludim is evidently the name of a people. <div eID="gen511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen512" type="x-p"/> Anamim - According to Bochart, the people who inhabited the district about the temple of Jupiter Ammon. <div eID="gen512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen513" type="x-p"/> Lehabim - The Libyans, or a people who dwelt on the west of the Thebaid, and were called Libyo-Egyptians. <div eID="gen513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen514" type="x-p"/> Naphtuhim - Even the conjectures can scarcely fix a place for these people. Bochart seems inclined to place them in Marmarica, or among the Troglodytae.
entries.5d6bc700f76425373a3d2405638ab847416fcb7a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen515" type="x-p"/> Pathrusim - The inhabitants of the Delta, in Egypt, according to the Chaldee paraphrase; but, according to Bochart, the people who inhabited the Thebaid, called Pathros in Scripture. <div eID="gen515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen516" type="x-p"/> Casluhim - The inhabitants of Colchis; for almost all authors allow that Colchis was peopled from Egypt. <div eID="gen516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen517" type="x-p"/> Philistim - The people called Philistines, the constant plagues and frequent oppressors of the Israelites, whose history may be seen at large in the books of Samuel, Kings, etc. <div eID="gen517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen518" type="x-p"/> Caphtorim - Inhabitants of Cyprus according to Calmet.
entries.357e4b06c7feb3160a2bee4976ed70ce52aa8eb5: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen519" type="x-p"/> Sidon - Who probably built the city of this name, and was the father of the Sidonians. <div eID="gen519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen520" type="x-p"/> Heth - From whom came the Hittites, so remarkable among the Canaanitish nations.
entries.e73cf705db1d24ccbf6c837976dbb3256ba0cc5c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen521" type="x-p"/> The Jebusite-Amorite, etc. - Are well known as being the ancient inhabitants of Canaan, expelled by the children of Israel.
entries.85dddf050b4dd8e77198243a64690939dedb61c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen522" type="x-p"/> These are the sons of Ham after their families - No doubt all these were well known in the days of Moses, and for a long time after; but at this distance, when it is considered that the political state of the world has been undergoing almost incessant revolutions through all the intermediate portions of time, the impossibility of fixing their residences or marking their descendants must be evident, as both the names of the people and the places of their residences have been changed beyond the possibility of being recognized.
entries.31c5e8c3b987a377f3d175ccba144d20d7ea32ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen523" type="x-p"/> Shem also, the father of all the children of Eber - It is generally supposed that the Hebrews derived their name from Eber or Heber, son of Shem; but it appears much more likely that they had it from the circumstance of Abraham passing over (for so the word עבר abar signifies) the river Euphrates to come into the land of Canaan. See the history of Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.13">Gen 14:13</reference> (note).
entries.d85aa0117f7d2a39c413fd0ec75f7b2605debe12: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen524" type="x-p"/> Elam - From whom came the Elamites, near to the Medes, and whose chief city was Elymais. <div eID="gen524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen525" type="x-p"/> Asshur - Who gave his name to a vast province (afterwards a mighty empire) called Assyria. <div eID="gen525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen526" type="x-p"/> Arphaxad - From whom Arrapachitis in Assyria was named, according to some; or Artaxata in Armenia, on the frontiers of Media, according to others. <div eID="gen526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen527" type="x-p"/> Lud - The founder of the Lydians. In Asia Minor; or of the Ludim, who dwelt at the confluence of the Euphrates and Tigris, according to Arias Montanus. <div eID="gen527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen528" type="x-p"/> Aram - The father of the Arameans, afterwards called Syrians.
entries.a5f7f0ab7cfad05fd1d511c488a92c7f89456c39: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen529" type="x-p"/> Uz - Who peopled Caelosyria, and is supposed to have been the founder of Damascus. <div eID="gen529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen530" type="x-p"/> Hul - Who peopled a part of Armenia. <div eID="gen530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen531" type="x-p"/> Gether - Supposed by Calmet to have been the founder of the Itureans, who dwelt beyond the Jordan, having Arabia Desert on the east, and the Jordan on the west. <div eID="gen531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen532" type="x-p"/> Mash - Who inhabited mount Masius in Mesopotamia, and from whom the river Mazeca, which has its source in that mountain, takes its name.
entries.51251180096e48fbf19d8916e129eb1f26b224bc: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen533" type="x-p"/> Salah - The founder of the people of Susiana. <div eID="gen533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen534" type="x-p"/> Eber - See <reference osisRef="Gen.10.21">Gen 10:21</reference>. The Septuagint add Cainan here, with one hundred and thirty to the chronology.
entries.2d62620091fa5d1c7da1ab7805d32ead76534494: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen535" type="x-p"/> Peleg - From פלג palag, to divide, because in his days, which is supposed to be about one hundred years after the flood, the earth was divided among the sons of Noah. Though some are of opinion that a physical division, and not a political one, is what is intended here, viz., a separation of continents and islands from the main land; the earthy parts having been united into one great continent previously to the days of Peleg. This opinion appears to me the most likely, for what is said, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.5">Gen 10:5</reference>, is spoken by way of anticipation.
entries.8e9cb0baa7a224d1c229dfb27796fb7b613ccd86: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen536" type="x-p"/> Joktan - He had thirteen sons who had their dwelling from Mesha unto Sephar, a mount of the east, which places Calmet supposes to be mount Masius, on the west in Mesopotamia, and the mountains of the Saphirs on the east in Armenia, or of the Tapyrs farther on in Media. In confirmation that all men have been derived from one family, let it be observed that there are many customs and usages, both sacred and civil, which have prevailed in all parts of the world; and that these could owe their origin to nothing but a general institution, which could never have existed, had not mankind been originally of the same blood, and instructed in the same common notions before they were dispersed. Among these usages may be reckoned, <div eID="gen536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen537" type="x-p"/> 1. The numbering by tens. <div eID="gen537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen538" type="x-p"/> 2. Their computing time by a cycle of seven days. <div eID="gen538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen539" type="x-p"/> 3. Their setting apart the seventh day for religious purposes. <div eID="gen539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen540" type="x-p"/> 4. Their use of sacrifices, propitiatory and eucharistical. <div eID="gen540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen541" type="x-p"/> 5. The consecration of temples and altars. <div eID="gen541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen542" type="x-p"/> 6. The institution of sanctuaries or places of refuge, and their privileges. <div eID="gen542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen543" type="x-p"/> 7. Their giving a tenth part of the produce of their fields, etc., for the use of the altar. <div eID="gen543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen544" type="x-p"/> 8. The custom of worshipping the Deity bare-footed. <div eID="gen544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen545" type="x-p"/> 9. Abstinence of the men from all sensual gratifications previously to their offering sacrifice. <div eID="gen545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen546" type="x-p"/> 10. The order of priesthood and its support. <div eID="gen546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen547" type="x-p"/> 11. The notion of legal pollutions, defilements, etc. <div eID="gen547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen548" type="x-p"/> 12. The universal tradition of a general deluge. <div eID="gen548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen549" type="x-p"/> 13. The universal opinion that the rainbow was a Divine sign, or portent, etc., etc. See Dodd. <div eID="gen549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen550" type="x-p"/> The wisdom and goodness of God are particularly manifested in repeopling the earth by means of three persons, all of the same family, and who had witnessed that awful display of Divine justice in the destruction of the world by the flood, while themselves were preserved in the ark. By this very means the true religion was propagated over the earth; for the sons of Noah would certainly teach their children, not only the precepts delivered to their father by God himself, but also how in his justice he had brought the flood on the world of the ungodly, and by his merciful providence preserved them from the general ruin. It is on this ground alone that we can account for the uniformity and universality of the above traditions, and for the grand outlines of religious truth which are found in every quarter of the world. God has so done his marvellous works that they may be had in everlasting remembrance.  <chapter eID="Gen.10"/> <div eID="gen550" type="x-p"/>

entries.6105cab5b1df91fffc0bf0b78b860845ebb5f507: <reference osisRef="Gen.10.1-Gen.10.5">Gen 10:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen160" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">IV. History of the Sons of Noah - Genesis 10-11:9</title> <title type="x-s2">Pedigree of the Nations - Genesis 10</title> <div sID="gen161" type="x-p"/> Of the sons of Noah, all that is handed down is the pedigree of the nations, or the list of the tribes which sprang from them (Gen 10), and the account of the confusion of tongues, together with the dispersion of men over the face of the earth (<reference osisRef="Gen.11.1-Gen.11.9">Gen 11:1-9</reference>); two events that were closely related to one another, and of the greatest importance to the history of the human race and of the kingdom of God. The genealogy traces the origin of the tribes which were scattered over the earth; the confusion of tongues shows the cause of the division of the one human race into many different tribes with peculiar languages.<hi type="italic">The genealogy of the tribes</hi> is not an ethnographical myth, nor the attempt of an ancient Hebrew to trace the connection of his own people with the other nations of the earth by means of uncertain traditions and subjective combinations, but a historical record of the Genesis of the nations, founded upon a tradition handed down from the fathers, which, to judge from its contents, belongs to the time of Abraham (cf. Hävernick’s <hi type="italic">Introduction to Pentateuch</hi>, pp. 118ff. transl.), and was inserted by Moses in the early history of the kingdom of God on account of its universal importance in connection with sacred history. For it not only indicates the place of the family which was chosen as the recipient of divine revelation among the rest of the nations, but traces the origin of the entire world, with the prophetical intention of showing that the nations, although they were quickly suffered to walk in their own ways (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.16">Act 14:16</reference>), were not intended to be for ever excluded from the counsels of eternal love. <div eID="gen161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen162" type="x-p"/> In this respect the genealogies prepare the way for the promise of the blessing, which was one day to spread from the chosen family to all the families of the earth (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.2-Gen.12.3">Gen 12:2-3</reference>). - The historical character of the genealogy is best attested by the contents themselves, since no trace can be detected, either of any pre-eminence given to the Shemites, or of an intention to fill up gaps by conjecture or invention. It gives just as much as had been handed down with regard to the origin of the different tribes. Hence the great diversity in the lists of the descendants of the different sons of Noah. Some are brought down only to the second, others to the third or fourth generation, and some even further; and whilst in several instances the founder of a tribe is named, in others we have only the tribes themselves; and in some cases we are unable to determine whether the names given denote the founder or the tribe. In many instances, too, on account of the defects and the unreliable character of the accounts handed down to us from different ancient sources with regard to the origin of the tribes, there are names which cannot be identified with absolute certainty.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Sam. Bochart</hi> has brought great learning to the explanation of the table of nations in <hi type="italic">Phaleg</hi>, the first part of his <hi type="italic">geographia sacra</hi>, to which <hi type="italic">Michaelis</hi> and <hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi> made valuable additions-the former in his spicil. geogr. Hebr. ext. 1769 and 1780, the latter in his Biblical Antiquities. <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> has made use of all the modern ethnographical discoveries in his “Völkertafel der Genesis” (1850), but many of his combinations are very speculative. <hi type="italic">Kiepert</hi>, in his article <hi type="italic">über d. geograph. Stellung der nördlichen Länder in der phönikisch-hebräischen Erdkunde </hi>(<hi type="italic">in the Monatsberichte d. Berliner</hi> Akad. 1859), denies entirely the ethnographical character of the table of nations, and reduces it to a mere attempt on the part of the Phoenicians to account for the geographical position of the nations with which they were acquainted.</note> <div eID="gen162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen163" type="x-p"/> Descendants of Japhet. - In <reference osisRef="Gen.10.1">Gen 10:1</reference> the names of the three sons are introduced according to their relative ages, to give completeness and finish to the <hi type="italic">Tholedoth</hi>; but in the genealogy itself Japhet is mentioned first and Shem last, according to the plan of the book of Genesis as already explained in the introduction. In <reference osisRef="Gen.10.2">Gen 10:2</reference> seven sons of Japhet are given. The names, indeed, afterwards occur as those of tribes; but here undoubtedly they are intended to denote the tribe-fathers, and may without hesitation be so regarded. For even if in later times many nations received their names from the lands of which they took possession, this cannot be regarded as a universal rule, since unquestionably the natural rule in the derivation of the names would be for the tribe to be called after its ancestor, and for the countries to receive their names from their earliest inhabitants. <hi type="italic">Gomer</hi> is most probably the tribe of the <hi type="italic">Cimmerians</hi>, who dwelt, according to <hi type="italic">Herodotus</hi>, on the Maeotis, in the Taurian Chersonesus, and from whom are descended the <hi type="italic">Cumri</hi> or <hi type="italic">Cymry</hi> in Wales and Brittany, whose relation to the Germanic <hi type="italic">Cimbri</hi> is still in obscurity. <hi type="italic">Magog</hi> is connected by <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> with the <hi type="italic">Scythians</hi> on the Sea of Asof and in the Caucasus; but <hi type="italic">Kiepert</hi> associates the name with <hi type="italic">Macija</hi> or <hi type="italic">Maka</hi>, and applies it to Scythian nomad tribes which forced themselves in between the Arian or Arianized Medes, Kurds, and Armenians. <hi type="italic">Madai</hi> are the Medes, called <hi type="italic">Mada</hi> on the arrow-headed inscriptions. Javan corresponds to the Greek Ἰάων, from whom the Ionians (Ἰάονος) are derived, the parent tribe of the Greeks (in Sanskrit <hi type="italic">Javana</hi>, old Persian <hi type="italic">Junâ</hi>). <hi type="italic">Tubal</hi> and <hi type="italic">Meshech</hi> are undoubtedly the <hi type="italic">Tibareni</hi> and <hi type="italic">Moschi</hi>, the former of whom are placed by Herodotus upon the east of the <hi type="italic">Thermodon</hi>, the latter between the sources of the Phasis and Cyrus. <hi type="italic">Tiras:</hi> according to Josephus, the <hi type="italic">Thracians</hi>, whom <hi type="italic">Herodotus</hi> calls the most numerous tribe next to the Indian. As they are here placed by the side of Meshech, so we also find on the old Egyptian monuments <hi type="italic">Mashuash</hi> and <hi type="italic">Tuirash</hi>, and upon the Assyrian <hi type="italic">Tubal</hi> and <hi type="italic">Misek</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rawlinson</hi>).
entries.eb61bd29f4f7bc35dbd10a7457bd83d13de1ef01: <reference osisRef="Gen.10.6-Gen.10.20">Gen 10:6-20</reference> <div eID="gen164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen165" type="x-p"/> Descendants of Ham. - <hi type="italic">Cush:</hi> the <hi type="italic">Ethiopians</hi> of the ancients, who not only dwelt in Africa, but were scattered over the whole of Southern Asia, and originally, in all probability, settled in Arabia, where the tribes that still remained, mingled with Shemites, and adopted a Shemitic language. <hi type="italic">Mizraim</hi> is <hi type="italic">Egypt</hi>: the dual form was probably transferred from the land to the people, referring, however, not to the <hi type="italic">double strip</hi>, i.e., the two strips of land into which the country is divided by the Nile, but to the two Egypts, Upper and Lower, two portions of the country which differ considerably in their climate and general condition. The name is obscure, and not traceable to any Semitic derivation; for the term מצור in <reference osisRef="Isa.19.6">Isa 19:6</reference>, etc., is not to be regarded as an etymological interpretation, but as a significant play upon the word. The old Egyptian name is <hi type="italic">Kemi</hi> (Copt. Chêmi, Kême), which, <hi type="italic">Plutarch</hi> says, is derived from the dark ash-grey colour of the soil covered by the slime of the Nile, but which it is much more correct to trace to <hi type="italic">Ham</hi>, and to regard as indicative of the Hamitic descent of its first inhabitants. <hi type="italic">Put</hi> denotes the <hi type="italic">Libyans</hi> in the wider sense of the term (old Egypt. <hi type="italic">Phet</hi>; Copt. <hi type="italic">Phaiat</hi>), who were spread over Northern Africa as far as Mauritania, where even in the time of Jerome a river with the neighbouring district still bore the name of <hi type="italic">Phut</hi>; cf. <hi type="italic">Bochart</hi>, Phal. iv. 33. On <hi type="italic">Canaan</hi>, see Gen 9:25.
entries.9da00d11cf2f5e919ee791e16853e9f9ade4827c: <reference osisRef="Gen.10.21-Gen.10.22">Gen 10:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen173" type="x-p"/> Descendants of Shem. - Gen 10:21. For the construction, vid., Gen 4:26. <hi type="italic">Shem</hi> is called the father of all the sons of <hi type="italic">Eber</hi>, because two tribes sprang from Eber through Peleg and Joktan, viz., the Abrahamides, and also the Arabian tribe of the Joktanides (Gen 4:26.). - On the expression, “<hi type="italic">the brother of Japhet</hi> הגּדול,” see Gen 9:24. The names of the five sons of Shem occur elsewhere as the names of the tribes and countries; at the same time, as there is no proof that in any single instance the name was transferred from the country to its earliest inhabitants, no well-grounded objection can be offered to the assumption, which the analogy of the other descendants of Shem renders probable, that they were originally the names of individuals. As the name of a people, <hi type="italic">Elam</hi> denotes the <hi type="italic">Elymaeans</hi>, who stretched from the Persian Gulf to the Caspian Sea, but who are first met with as Persians no longer speaking a Semitic language. <hi type="italic">Asshur:</hi> the <hi type="italic">Assyrians</hi> who settled in the country of <hi type="italic">Assyria</hi>, Ἀτουρία, to the east of the Tigris, but who afterwards spread in the direction of Asia Minor. <hi type="italic">Arphaxad:</hi> the inhabitants of Ἀῤῥαπαχῖχτις in northern Assyria. The explanation given of the name, viz., “fortress of the Chaldeans” (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>), “highland of the Chaldeans” (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>), “territory of the Chaldeans” (<hi type="italic">Dietrich</hi>), are very questionable. <hi type="italic">Lud:</hi> the <hi type="italic">Lydians</hi> of Asia Minor, whose connection with the Assyrians is confirmed by the names of the ancestors of their kings. <hi type="italic">Aram:</hi> the ancestor of the <hi type="italic">Aramaeans</hi> of Syria and Mesopotamia.
entries.a03795bde9b46f691d205decc431a70b9b19a15f: <reference osisRef="Gen.10.23-Gen.10.24">Gen 10:23-24</reference> <hi type="italic">Descendants of Aram.</hi> <hi type="italic">Uz:</hi> a name which occurs among the <hi type="italic">Nahorides</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.21">Gen 22:21</reference>) and Horites (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.28">Gen 36:28</reference>), and which is associated with the Αἰσῖται of Ptolemy, in <hi type="italic">Arabia deserta</hi> towards Babylon; this is favoured by the fact that <hi type="italic">Uz</hi>, the country of Job, is called by the lxx χώρα Αὐσῖτις, although the notion that these <hi type="italic">Aesites</hi> were an Aramaean tribe, afterwards mixed up with Nahorides and Horites, is mere conjecture. <hi type="italic">Hul:</hi> <hi type="italic">Delitzsch</hi> associates this with <hi type="italic">Cheli</hi> (<hi type="italic">Cheri</hi>), the old Egyptian name for the Syrians, and the <hi type="italic">Hylatae</hi> who dwelt near the Emesenes (Plin. 5, 19). <hi type="italic">Gether</hi> he connects with the name give in the Arabian legends to the ancestor of the tribes <hi type="italic">Themûd</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ghadis</hi>. <hi type="italic">Mash:</hi> for which we find <hi type="italic">Meshech</hi> in <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.17">1Ch 1:17</reference>, a tribe mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ps.120.5">Psa 120:5</reference> along with Kedar, and since the time of <hi type="italic">Bochart</hi> generally associated with the πορος Μάσιον above <hi type="italic">Nisibis</hi>.
entries.27f46dd1157f52eeb89eb117cae5753a9162ae07: <reference osisRef="Gen.10.25-Gen.10.29">Gen 10:25-29</reference> <div eID="gen173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen174" type="x-p"/> Among the descendants of Arphaxad, Eber’s eldest son received the name of <hi type="italic">Peleg</hi>, because in his days the earth, i.e., the population of the earth, was divided, in consequence of the building of the tower of Babel (<reference osisRef="Gen.11.8">Gen 11:8</reference>). His brother <hi type="italic">Joktan</hi> is called Kachtan by the Arabians, and is regarded as the father of all the primitive tribes of Arabia. The names of his sons are given in <reference osisRef="Gen.10.26">Gen 10:26</reference>-29. There are thirteen of them, some of which are still retained in places and districts of Arabia, whilst others are not yet discovered, or are entirely extinct. Nothing certain has been ascertained about <hi type="italic">Almodad, Jerah, Diklah, Obal, Abimael,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jobab</hi>. Of the rest, <hi type="italic">Sheleph</hi> is identical with <hi type="italic">Salif</hi> or <hi type="italic">Sulaf</hi> (in Ptl. 6, 7, Σαλαπηνοί), an old Arabian tribe, also a district of <hi type="italic">Yemen</hi>. <hi type="italic">Hazarmaveth</hi> (i.e., forecourt of death) is the Arabian <hi type="italic">Hadhramaut</hi> in South-eastern Arabia on the Indian Ocean, whose name <hi type="italic">Jauhari</hi> is derived from the unhealthiness of the climate. <hi type="italic">Hadoram:</hi> the Ἀδραμῖται of Ptol. 6, 7, <hi type="italic">Atramitae</hi> of Plin. 6, 28, on the southern coast of Arabia. <hi type="italic">Uzal:</hi> one of the most important towns of <hi type="italic">Yemen</hi>, south-west of <hi type="italic">Mareb</hi>. <hi type="italic">Sheba:</hi> the <hi type="italic">Sabaeans</hi>, with the capital <hi type="italic">Saba</hi> or <hi type="italic">Mareb</hi>, <hi type="italic">Mariaba</hi> <hi type="italic">regia</hi> (Plin.), whose connection with the Cushite (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.7">Gen 10:7</reference>) and <hi type="italic">Abrahamite</hi> Sabaeans (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.3">Gen 25:3</reference>) is quite in obscurity. <hi type="italic">Ophir</hi> has not yet been discovered in Arabia; it is probably to be sought on the Persian Gulf, even if the Ophir of Solomon was not situated there. <hi type="italic">Havilah</hi> appears to answer to <hi type="italic">Chaulaw</hi> of <hi type="italic">Edrisi</hi>, a district between Sanaa and Mecca. But this district, which lies in the heart of Yemen, does not fit the account in <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.7">1Sa 15:7</reference>, nor the statement in <reference osisRef="Gen.25.18">Gen 25:18</reference>, that Havilah formed the boundary of the territory of the Ishmaelites. These two passages point rather to Χαυλοταῖοι, a place on the border of Arabia Petraea towards Yemen, between the Nabataeans and Hagrites, which Strabo describes as habitable.
entries.6744a145dd0ba8ac4d758831f1a336ff8a01b249: <reference osisRef="Gen.10.30-Gen.10.31">Gen 10:30-31</reference> <div eID="gen174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen175" type="x-p"/> The settlements of these Joktanides lay “<hi type="italic">from Mesha towards Sephar the mountain of the East,</hi>” <hi type="italic">Mesha</hi> is still unknown: according to Gesenius, it is <hi type="italic">Mesene</hi> on the Persian Gulf, and in <hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> opinion, it is the valley of <hi type="italic">Bisha</hi> or <hi type="italic">Beishe</hi> in the north of Yemen; but both are very improbable. <hi type="italic">Sepher</hi> is supposed by <hi type="italic">Mesnel</hi> to be the ancient Himyaritish capital, <hi type="italic">Shafâr</hi>, on the Indian Ocean; and the <hi type="italic">mountain of the East</hi>, the mountain of incense, which is situated still farther to the east. - The genealogy of the Shemites closes with <reference osisRef="Gen.10.31">Gen 10:31</reference>, and the entire genealogy of the nations with Gen 10:32. According to the Jewish Midrash, there are seventy tribes, with as many different languages; but this number can only be arrived at by reckoning Nimrod among the Hamites, and not only placing Peleg among the Shemites, but taking his ancestors Salah and Eber to be names of separate tribes. By this we obtain for Japhet 14, for Ham 31, and for Shem 25, - in all 70 names. The Rabbins, on the other hand, reckon 14 Japhetic, 30 Hamitic, and 26 Semitic nations; whilst the fathers make 72 in all. But as these calculations are perfectly arbitrary, and the number 70 is nowhere given or hinted at, we can neither regard it as intended, nor discover in it “the number of the divinely appointed varieties of the human race,” or “of the cosmical development,” even if the seventy disciples (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.1">Luk 10:1</reference>) were meant to answer to the seventy nations whom the Jews supposed to exist upon the earth.
entries.0d176f84d00d29d0ebf8d988c5aef5d9c2a728db: <reference osisRef="Gen.10.32">Gen 10:32</reference> <div eID="gen175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen176" type="x-p"/> The words, “<hi type="italic">And by these were the nations of the earth divided in the earth after the flood,</hi>” prepare the way for the description of that event which led to the division of the one race into many nations with different languages.  <chapter eID="Gen.10"/> <div eID="gen176" type="x-p"/>

entries.1b8b82892b81709addc0c478fd310ab05c36cf08: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.10.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.10.1" sID="gen1454" type="section"/> <div sID="gen1455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">These</hi> <hi type="italic">are</hi> <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">generations</hi> . If any one pleases more accurately to examine the genealogies related by Moses in this and the following chapter, I do not condemn his industry. <note n="306"> <div sID="gen1456" type="x-p"/> For ample information on this interesting subject, which the general plan of Calvin’s Commentary scarcely allowed him fully to investigate, the reader cannot do better than consult Dr. Wells’ Geography of the Old Testament, chap. 3 From certain expressiones contained in the Mosaic account here given, of the first settlement of nations after the flood, it is clear that the records of the chapter now before us, have reference to the state of things after the confusion of tongues at the building of the Tower of Babel, though the narration of this event occurs in the chapter following; for the settlements are said to be made “according to their languages.” But we know that before the attempt to build the tower, the whole earth was of “one language and of one speech;” and therefore the events here placed first, in the order of narration, were subsequent in the order of time. It may be proper here to observe, that according to the division of the earth into three great portions, Europe, Asia, and Africa, speaking generally, Japheth was the progenitor of the Europeans, Shem of the Asiatics, and Ham of the Africans. Yet this line of demarcation is not intended to be accurately drawn. The whole of Lesser Asia, for instance, falls within the province of the sons of Japheth; and Arabia within that of the sons of Ham. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen1456" type="x-p"/> </note> And some interpreters have not unsuccessfully applied their diligence and study to this point. Let them enjoy, as far as I am concerned the reward of their labors. It shall, however, suffice for me briefly to allude to those things which I deem more useful to be noticed, and for the sake of which I suppose these genealogies to have been written by Moses. First, in these bare names we have still some fragment of the history of the world; and the next chapter will show how many years intervened between the date of the deluge and the time when God made his covenant with Abraham. This second commencement of mankind is especially worthy to be known; and detestable is the ingratitude of those, who, when they had heard, from their fathers and grandfathers of the wonderful restoration of the world in so short a time, yet voluntarily became forgetful of the grace and the salvation of God. Even the memory of the deluge was by the greater part entirely lost. Very few cared by what means or for what end they had been preserved. Many ages afterwards, seeing that the wicked forgetfulness of men had rendered them callous to the judgment and mercy of God, the door was opened to the lies of Satan by whose artifice it came to pass, that heathen poets scattered abroad futile and even noxious fables, by which the truth respecting God’s works was adulterated. The goodness of God, therefore, wonderfully triumphed over the wickedness of men, in having granted a prolongation of life to beings so ungrateful, brutal, and barbarous. Now, to captious men, (who yet do not think it absurd to refuse to acknowledge a Creator of the world,) such a sudden increase of mankind seems incredible, and therefore they ridicule it as fabulous. I grant, indeed, that if we choose to estimate what Moses relates by our own reason, it may be regarded as a fable; but they act very perversely who do not attend to the design of the Holy Spirit. For what else, I ask, did the Spirit intend, than that the offspring of three men should be increased, not by natural means, or in a common manner, but by the unwonted exercise of the power of God, for the purpose of replenishing the earth far and wide? They who regard this miracle of God as fabulous on account of its magnitude, should much less believe that Noah and his sons, with their wives, breathed in the waters, and that animals lived nearly a whole year without sun and air. This then, is a gigantic madness, <note n="307"> <div sID="gen1457" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="la">Hic ergo Cyclopicus est furor</foreign>.”<div eID="gen1457" type="x-p"/> </note> to hold up to ridicule what is said respecting the restoration of the human race: for there the admirable power of God is displayed. How much better would it be, in the history of these events, — which Noah saw with his own eyes, and not without great admiration, — to behold God, to admire his power, to celebrate his goodness, and to acknowledge his hand, not less filled with mysteries in restoring, than in creating the world? We must, however, observe, that in the three catalogues which Moses furnishes, <note n="308"> <div sID="gen1458" type="x-p"/> The first relating to the sons of Japheth the elder brother, from verse 2 to verse 6; the second, to the sons of Ham, from verse 6 to verse 21; the third, to the sons of Shem, from 21 to the end. Shem, though generally named first as a mark of Divine favor, is here placed last, because the subsequent history of Moses principally concerns this race; as Calvin properly argues. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen1458" type="x-p"/> </note> all the heads of the families are not enumerated; but those only, among the grandsons of Noah, are recorded, who were the princes of nations. For as any one excelled among his brethren, in talent, valor, industry, or other endowments, he obtained for himself a name and power, so that others, resting under his shadow, freely conceded to him the priority. Therefore, among the sons of Japheth, of Ham, and of Shem, Moses enumerates those only who had been celebrated, and by whose names the people were called. Moreover, although no certain cause appears why Moses begins at Japheth, and descends in the second place to Ham, yet it is probable that the first place is given to the sons of Japheth, because they, having wandered over many regions, and having even crossed the sea, had receded farther from their country: and since these nations were less known to the Jews, therefore he alludes to them briefly. He assigns the second place to the sons of Ham, the knowledge of whom, on account of their vicinity, was more familiar to the Jews. But since he had determined to weave the history of the Church in one continuous narrative, he postpones the progeny of Shem, from which the church flowed, to the last place. Wherefore, the order in which they are mentioned is not that of dignity; since Moses puts those first, whom he wished slightly to pass over, as obscure. Besides, we must observe, that the children of this world are exalted for a time, so that the whole earth seems as if it were made for their benefit, but their glory being transient vanishes away; while the Church, in an ignoble and despised condition, as if creeping on the ground, is yet divinely preserved, until at length, in his own time, God shall lift up her head. I have already declared that I leave to others the scrupulous investigation of the names here mentioned. The reason of certain of them is manifest from the Scripture, such as Cush, Mizraim, Madai, Canaan, and the like: in respect to some others there are probable conjectures; in others, the obscurity is too great to allow of any certain conclusion; and those figments which interpreters adduce are, in part, very much distorted and forced; in part, vapid, and without any fair pretext. Undoubtedly it seems to be the part of a frivolous curiosity to seek for certain and distinct nations in each of these names. <note n="309"> <div sID="gen1459" type="x-p"/> Doubtless there is truth in these remarks of Calvin. Yet he seems to carry his objection too far. For it is one of the strongest possible confirmations of the truth of the Mosaic history, that (notwithstanding some inevitable obscurity) there should be such a mass of undeniable evidence still existing, that the world was really divided in the manner here described. Far more nations than Calvin supposed may, with the highest degree of probability, be traced upward to the progenitors whose names are here recorded. See Wells’ Geography, Mede’s Works, and Bishop Patrick’s Commentary. A list of the names, with the supposed corresponding nations, is also given in the Commentary of Professor Bush on this chapter.
